title: Worn Tiles
statement: A hallway has length floor tiles, numbered 0 to length - 1. A cleaning pass [from, to] scrubs every tile from from to to, both ends included. A tile wears out once at least limit passes have scrubbed it. Passes may overlap, repeat or touch each other in any order. Return how many tiles are worn out after all the passes.
constraints: 0 <= from <= to < length for every pass

examples.explanation: Tiles 4, 5 and 6 are covered by two or more passes (tile 5 by three), and tiles 8 and 9 are covered by the second and fourth passes. That makes 5 worn tiles. Every other tile is scrubbed at most once.
One pass scrubs every tile exactly once, so no tile reaches the limit of 2.

hints.content: Focus on one tile. What do you need to know about it, and at which moments while walking along the hallway does that number change?

Painting every tile of every pass costs about the sum of all pass lengths, hundreds of millions of writes in the worst case. The pass count of a tile only changes where a pass begins or just after one ends.
Keep an array change with one slot more than the hallway. A pass adds 1 at its first tile and subtracts 1 at the tile right after its last tile.
Walk left to right with a running sum of change. At each tile the running sum is exactly the number of passes covering it.
Count the tiles whose running sum is at least limit. The slot at index length absorbs the subtraction of a pass that ends at the last tile. Time is O(length + passes), space O(length).

testCases.explanation: Five tiles are scrubbed at least twice.
A single pass never reaches a limit of 2.
No passes, so nothing wears out.
Repeated passes over the only tile reach the limit exactly.
Passes that touch end to end never overlap, so no tile is scrubbed twice.
Only the two tiles under all three passes reach the limit.
A medium random layout with many overlaps.
The largest size with passes covering almost the whole hallway: more than 300 million tile visits for a paint-every-tile loop.
The largest size with random long passes spread over the hallway.
Short passes near the far end of a very long hallway, written with five-digit coordinates.

solutions.title: Paint every tile of every pass
solutions.intuition: Keep a counter per tile and add one to every tile a pass scrubs.
solutions.approach: For each pass, loop from its first to its last tile and increment that tile's counter. Finally count the tiles whose counter is at least limit.
solutions.pseudocode:
scrubbed = [0] * length
for (from, to) in passes: for tile in from..to: scrubbed[tile] += 1
return count of tiles with scrubbed[tile] >= limit
solutions.timeComplexity: O(length + total length of all passes), up to 3,500 * 100,000 = 350 million steps
commonMistakes: Stopping the inner loop at to - 1 and missing the last tile of every pass.
Counting passes instead of worn tiles at the end.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is the direct simulation of the story and is correct for any input. Its cost is the total length of the passes, which can be 3,500 passes over 100,000 tiles, far too slow. The pass count only changes at pass edges, which is what the faster solutions use.

steps.title: Paint the first pass
steps.content: Pass [2, 6] adds one to tiles 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

steps.title: Paint the rest and count
steps.content: After all four passes the counters at tiles 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9 are at least 2, so the result is 5.

solutions.title: Sort the pass edges and sweep
solutions.intuition: The covered count only changes at a pass start or just after a pass end, so sort those edges and add up the lengths of the stretches where the count is at least limit.
solutions.approach: Collect all starts and all end + 1 values, sort each list, and merge them in order. Before processing an edge, if the active pass count is at least limit, add the distance since the previous edge to the answer. Then apply every start and end sitting at that edge.
solutions.pseudocode:
opens = sorted(from); closes = sorted(to + 1)
active = 0; at = 0; worn = 0
while edges remain: edge = smaller next edge
  if active >= limit: worn += edge - at
  at = edge; active += starts at edge; active -= ends at edge
solutions.timeComplexity: O(passes log passes), independent of the hallway length
commonMistakes: Using the end coordinate instead of end + 1, which drops the last tile of a pass.
Processing a start and an end at the same edge in the wrong order before measuring the stretch.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Only the passes matter when the hallway is huge and the passes are few, so this version never touches individual tiles. The sort costs O(p log p); the difference-array solution needs O(length) memory but no sort, which wins when passes are many and the hallway is short.

steps.title: Edges
steps.content: For the first example the starts are 2, 4, 5 and 8 and the exclusive ends are 7, 10, 6 and 12.

steps.title: Sweep
steps.content: The count is 2 from edge 4 to edge 5 (tile 4), 3 from 5 to 6 (tile 5), 2 from 6 to 7 (tile 6) and 2 from 8 to 10 (tiles 8 and 9), so the worn tiles are 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5.

solutions.title: Difference array and a running sum
solutions.intuition: Record only where each pass starts and stops; the running sum of those marks is the pass count of every tile.
solutions.approach: Allocate change of size length + 1. For each pass add 1 at from and subtract 1 at to + 1. Sweep the tiles left to right keeping a running total of change and count the tiles where it is at least limit.
solutions.pseudocode:
change = [0] * (length + 1)
for (from, to) in passes: change[from] += 1; change[to + 1] -= 1
running = 0; worn = 0
for tile in 0..length-1: running += change[tile]; if running >= limit: worn += 1
commonMistakes: Making change only length long, so a pass ending at the last tile writes out of bounds.
Subtracting at to instead of to + 1, which drops the last scrubbed tile.
Resetting the running sum for each pass instead of keeping one sum for the whole sweep.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A pass is an interval, and the number of passes covering a tile is the sum of +1 marks at or before it minus -1 marks before it. A difference array stores those marks, and one prefix-sum sweep rebuilds every tile's count. That turns 350 million paint steps into about 103,500 operations.

steps.title: Mark the edges
steps.content: For the first example the marks are +1 at tiles 2, 4, 5 and 8 and -1 at tiles 7, 10, 6 and 12.

steps.title: Sweep and count
steps.content: The running sum reaches 2 at tile 4, 3 at tile 5, 2 at tile 6, drops at tile 7, is 2 again at tiles 8 and 9, so 5 tiles meet the limit.
